source: Research for the all-of-Grade-2-add-and-subtract pass, 2026-10-02: standards codes (src/standards, unknownCodes clean; our own summaries in g2-addsub-codes.json), the computation type table, difficulty rule and slips (research-computation.md), the app survey (research-app.md: what a bare model can draw today, the version switch, the topic), and the official Virginia (2023) and Georgia Grade 2 text read for decision 8. Written after Sai's comments on the word problem page asked that all of Grade 2 adding and subtracting be covered in this pass; revised after a second review round. Revised again 2026-10-02 after Sai's 17:54 and 18:21 UTC comments (no items served by state; keep the state lines, even when only one state prescribes something) and a review round: decisions 6 and 11 settled, row 35 on subskill tenOrHundredTo1200 (recommended), row 33's number rule fixed and its hint kept off the key, row 34's keys labelled in words, and no 'serve to' sentences.
note: Sai approved both Grade 2 add and subtract lists as recommended on 2026-10-02 ("approve both lists as recommended"). Status is decided in the database. mode_id is multiDigit, the new v2-only topic of decision 1; models and script-built items for these rows use it as modeId. A reload never overwrites an approved row, so the topic is settled before approval. Examples are our own, with numbers within 100 (rows 1-15, 28-34), past 100 to 200 (rows 17, 19), within 1,000 (rows 16, 18, 20-27) and up to 1,200 (row 35, Texas). Rows 33-35 are state lines with no Common Core code; every kid sees them (no state filter, Sai 2026-10-02 17:54 UTC), and their state codes are tags. Row 35 uses subskill tenOrHundredTo1200 (decision 11, recommended). Sai, 2026-10-02 18:21 UTC: keep the state lines, even when only one state prescribes something (decision 11 settled). spec.slips lists each named slip with its value for the example; spec.variantMistakes and spec.variantExamples give a variant its own slips and example where the row's slips can't happen. The chooseExpression and chooseSymbol formats and the regroup value 'two' are proposed taxonomy additions.

rows.title: Add two numbers within 100
rows.example: 68 + 25 = ? [93] (the regroup model)

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: two two-digit numbers, or a two-digit and a one-digit number; the sum at most 100; one model per variant

spec.why: 2.NBT.B.5: add within 100 with place-value strategies, the core Grade 2 computation.
spec.display: stacked in columns. The prompt is the bare equation (a + b = ?) and carries a, b and op, so web and iPhone stack it; a sentence prompt ('What is …?') shows in a row. A model may show some fills in a row with display.layout 'horizontal'
rules: misalignedPlaces only on fills with a one-digit number (57 + 6 answered 117).
variants: no regrouping: whole tens (50 + 30), a two-digit and a one-digit number (43 + 5), two two-digit numbers (easy)

rows.title: Subtract within 100
rows.example: 81 − 47 = ? [34] (the trade-a-ten model)

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: first number 20-99, difference at least 2; one model per variant

slips.says: took the smaller digit from the larger

spec.why: 2.NBT.B.5: subtract within 100. Subtracting across a ten is new in Grade 2.
spec.display: stacked in columns. The prompt is the bare equation (a + b = ?) and carries a, b and op, so web and iPhone stack it; a sentence prompt ('What is …?') shows in a row. A model may show some fills in a row with display.layout 'horizontal'
rules: smallerFromLarger and offByTen give the same number when the two ones digits differ by 5 (63 − 28 gives 45 both ways). Constrain those fills so the two slips differ.
variants: trade a ten, including a one-digit number taken across a ten, 53 − 7 (moderate)
a zero in the ones, 60 − 24, one trade (moderate)

rows.title: Add and take away in one line
rows.problem_type: Two steps in one line (a − b + c)

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: first number 30-99; the middle result and the answer within 100; one of the two steps uses a one-digit number; at most one step regroups; the signs are take away then add (58 − 23 + 7) or take away twice (64 − 21 − 8); about half the items regroup in one step

spec.why: Two steps in one line with the box at the end has nothing missing but the answer, so it is a computing item. It moved here from the word problem list and keeps that list's two-step limits (2.NBT.B.5; FL MA.2.AR.2.2 names equations with three or four numbers).
spec.display: in a row (display.layout 'horizontal')
rules: Leave out 'add then take away' (a + b − c): there the wrong-operation slip and the add-everything slip are the same number.

rows.title: Which sum is the same? Friendlier numbers
rows.example: Which is equal to 49 + 36? Choices: 50 + 36 (changed one number); 50 + 35; 40 + 30 + 6 (left out the 9 ones); 50 + 37 (changed both the wrong way). [50 + 35]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: one number 1 or 2 below a ten (29, 48), the other 11-59; the sum at most 100

spec.why: Moving 1 from one number to the other keeps the sum (2.NBT.B.5, properties). Picking the equal form is how this list checks 2.NBT.B.9's 'why it works'.
rules: Exactly one choice equals the sum. Each wrong choice is off by its named slip.

rows.title: Which difference is the same? Friendlier numbers
rows.example: Which is equal to 63 − 29? Choices: 63 − 30 (changed one number); 62 − 30 (changed both the wrong way); 64 − 30; 63 − 20 + 9 (added the 9). [64 − 30]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: the number taken away is 1 or 2 below a ten; the first number 30-99; the difference at least 10

spec.why: Same difference is a different rule from same sum (move both numbers the same way), with its own slips (2.NBT.B.5, 2.NBT.B.9).
rules: Exactly one choice equals the difference. Each wrong choice is off by its named slip.

rows.title: Add on a number line: hops of ten, then ones
rows.picture: number line with hops of ten, then one hop of ones; the landing point not labelled
rows.example: What is 54 + 28? [number line 50 to 90: hops from 54 to 64, 64 to 74, then 8 more; the landing point is not labelled] [82]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

rows.title: Subtract on a number line by counting up
rows.picture: number line with one hop from the smaller number to the larger
rows.example: What is 75 − 38? [number line 30 to 80, one hop from 38 to 75] [37]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: two numbers 11-99, difference 11-49 with one trade; the line runs from the ten at or below the smaller number to the ten at or above the larger, at most 50 wide

slips.says: took the smaller digit from the larger

spec.why: 2.MD.B.6: a difference shown as the distance between two numbers, found by counting up. Word problem row 24 draws the same one-hop line for a box equation; this row asks for a difference and carries the computing codes.
spec.display: numberLine in lineMode 'jump', one hop
rules: When the several-hop line (the row above) is built, a count-back model (hops of ten, then ones, to the left) can join this row.

rows.title: Check with the other operation
rows.problem_type: Check a subtraction with an addition (or the reverse)
rows.example: Which can you use to check 62 − 27 = 35? Choices: 35 + 27 = 62; 62 + 27 = 89 (added to the start); 35 − 27 = 8 (subtracted again). [35 + 27 = 62]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: two-digit numbers; the start plus the number taken away stays within 100, so every choice does too; the kid judges which sentence checks the work and does not compute it, so the row is moderate whether or not it trades; one model per variant

spec.why: 2.NBT.B.5 and GA 2.NR.2.4 name how adding and subtracting are related; checking with the other operation uses it.
rules: Every choice is true arithmetic, so the kid has to judge which one checks the work, not which one is right.

rows.title: Find the mistake in someone's work
rows.example: Ava says 57 + 26 = 73. What mistake did Ava make? Choices: Ava did not add the new ten from 7 + 6; Ava added the ones wrong (the 3 ones are right); Ava took away instead of adding (57 − 26 is 31); Ava made no mistake (kept Ava's answer). [Ava did not add the new ten from 7 + 6]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: the right answer needs one trade, and the shown answer is that trade's named slip; one model per variant

slips.value: Ava took away instead of adding

variantExamples.subtraction: the shown answer took the s: Leo says 74 − 38 = 44. What mistake did Leo make? Choices: Leo took 4 from 8 in the ones instead of trading a ten; Leo traded a ten but kept 7 tens (that slip gives 46); Leo added instead of taking away (74 + 38 is 112); Leo made no mistake (kept Leo's answer). [Leo took 4 from 8 in the ones instead of trading a ten]

spec.why: 2.NBT.B.9 asks kids to explain why a strategy works; naming the step that went wrong is that skill run in reverse. Research §4.10 finds finding the slip in someone's work the most telling bare item for place value.
spec.display: in a row; four text choices: check the layout with layoutSweep and the iPhone simulator, since both draw choices two to a row
rules: The shown answer is always one named slip (forgot to carry, or took the smaller digit from the larger), never a random number.
The wrong choices blame a place that was done right, another slip that gives a different answer, the operation, or nothing.
The person is named from NAMES, with no pronoun.
variants: addition: the shown answer forgot to carry (Ava says 57 + 26 = 73)
subtraction: the shown answer took the smaller digit from the larger (Leo says 74 − 38 = 44)

rows.title: Find the missing digit
rows.picture: none, numbers in a row with one digit boxed
rows.example: What digit goes in the box? 4□ + 27 = 73 [6]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: the boxed digit is in the ones of the first number, and the ones trade; one model per variant

spec.why: The ones of 73 can only come from a ones total of 13, so the kid reasons about the trade, which 2.NBT.B.9 asks kids to explain. No Grade 2 test asks this form, so it is the weakest row (decision 7).
spec.display: in a row; a box inside stacked columns needs build

rows.title: Which trade do you need? (disc mat)
rows.picture: tappable place-value disc mat (tens and ones), starting at the first number
rows.answer_format: build on the mat (the number the mat shows)
rows.example: The mat shows 75. Take away 36 on the mat. Trade only if you need to. What is 75 − 36? [the kid breaks 1 ten into 10 ones, then takes away 3 tens and 6 ones] [39]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: the mat starts at a two-digit number; about half the fills need one trade; one model per variant

slips.says: counted the broken ten as one of the tens taken away
took away one one disc too few

spec.why: 2.NBT.B.9 asks why strategies work, and the trade is the reason; the mat makes it visible. This is the picture row for computing within 100.
spec.display: the placeValueDiscs widget in build mode: display { mode: "build", cols: [{place, count}, …] }, the start mat; the answer is the number the finished mat shows
rules: The prompt states the number on the mat.
About half the fills need a trade and half do not, so the kid decides.
Sai chose a tappable mat on 2026-10-03 (the picture-only mat asked the kid to ignore it): the kid changes the mat and the answer is the number it shows.
variants: subtract: break a ten for 10 ones when the ones are short
add: trade 10 ones for 1 ten when the ones make 10 or more

numbers.note: two-digit numbers within 100; every false choice needs a trade, so it can show its slip, which makes the row moderate; the true choice trades in about half the items

slips.says: took the smaller digit from the larger

spec.why: FL MA.2.AR.2.1 asks kids to decide whether an equation within 100 is true, and VA 2.CE.1j whether two values are equal. Picking the true one works today while Yes/No waits.
rules: Exactly one choice is true. Each false choice is off by one named slip.
The reversed form (a number, then =, then the sum) appears on a false choice at least as often as on the true one, so the odd-looking form never gives the key away.

spec.objective: The equal sign within 100: both sides, true or false, equal or not

spec.why: VA 2.CE.1j asks whether two values are equal using models, and a trade keeps the value the same, the reason behind 2.NBT.B.9's strategies. The picture row for the equal sign. No Texas, Florida or Georgia code: none asks for equal or not equal with models.

rows.title: About how much? Best estimate (Virginia)
rows.problem_type: Estimate a sum or a difference
rows.example: About how much is 57 + 21? Choices: 70 (rounded both down); 80; 90 (rounded both up); 100 (rounded to the hundred). [80]

spec.objective: Add and subtract within 100 with place-value strategies, including up to four numbers

numbers.note: The estimate itself never trades: it adds or subtracts whole tens. Sums: two numbers 11-89, each 1 to 3 away from its nearest ten, one rounding up and the other down, their ones adding to 8 or 9 (no regrouping), the exact sum 50 or more, the estimate 60 to 80. Differences: the first number's ones are 1-3 and the second's 7-9, the two distances add to at most 4, the first number's ten is at least 20 more than the second's, and the two tens add to at most 100. The exact difference always trades (62 − 28), and only the hint's route works it; an estimate stays easy. The 'added' choice is the sum of the two rounded numbers. Either way, rounding each number and rounding the exact answer give the same ten, and the four choices differ; one model per variant

variantExamples.difference, 62 − 28 (easy): About how much is 62 − 28? Choices: 30; 40 (rounded one number the wrong way); 50 (rounded both the wrong way); 90 (added). [30]

spec.why: VA 2.CE.1a asks Grade 2 kids to estimate sums and differences; Common Core has no Grade 2 estimating. The bare form of word problem row 33.

state.asks: Virginia 2.CE.1a asks Grade 2 kids to estimate sums and differences with numbers up to 100; Common Core has no Grade 2 estimating.

rules: For a difference, 'rounded both down' and 'rounded both up' give the same number, so the difference model uses its own slips.

The hint's steps say to work the exact answer, then ask which ten it is closest to, and stop there; only the worked solution names the closest ten (the hint-leak check fails a hint that states the key). The exact answer is always within 4 of that ten, so any kid can answer without rounding (every kid sees this row, decision 11).

rows.title: = or ≠? (Virginia)
rows.problem_type: Equal or not equal, with the ≠ sign
rows.example: Which sign goes in the circle? 47 + 25 ○ 62. Choices: = (did not carry, so got 62); ≠. [≠]

spec.objective: The equal sign within 100: both sides, true or false, equal or not

numbers.note: a two-digit sum or difference on one side and a number on the other, within 100; about half the pairs are equal; a pair that is not equal is off by one named slip

spec.why: VA 2.CE.1i and 2.CE.1j ask for the ≠ sign; Common Core and the other states use = only. A number on one side keeps it moderate, as the true-or-false rows are split.

state.asks: Virginia 2.CE.1i and 2.CE.1j ask Grade 2 kids to use the ≠ sign; Common Core and the other states use = only.

spec.app: needs build: a ≠ key (the symbol keys are fixed to <, = and >), each key with its word under the sign, and a two-choice answer, blocked like Yes/No
rules: The two answer keys carry their words, = (equal) and ≠ (not equal), so a kid who has not met ≠ can answer without the hint (every kid sees this row, decision 11). No nudge, step or feedback line writes = or ≠, and no step writes an equation with an = sign, because the hint-leak check fails a fill whose key is that sign; the steps say to work out the side with two numbers, then compare it with the other side.
